lines.trans: Chef, why are you smiling so cheerfully?
Look into the courtyard at the neighboring restaurant.
A strict inspection just arrived over there!
Yes, that is a special service arriving.

words.gram: particle in the set phrase да ну

lines.trans: Did you call this inspection yourself?
Of course, they must respect the rules of order.
Now their cooks will be running around a lot.
Let them quickly run around the building!
Elena Pavlovna will be extremely furious.
She should not have parked her car here.
This is indeed very cruel little revenge.
This is a fair lesson for insolent neighbors.
Then let us calmly watch out the window!
Chef, why are you smiling so cheerfully?
Look into the courtyard at the neighboring restaurant.
A strict inspection just arrived over there!
Yes, that is a special service arriving.

Of course, they must respect the rules of order.
Now their cooks will be running around a lot.
Let them quickly run around the building!

She should not have parked her car here.

Of course, they must respect the rules of order.
Now their cooks will be running around a lot.
Let them quickly run around the building!
Elena Pavlovna will be extremely furious.
She should not have parked her car here.
This is indeed very cruel little revenge.

Then let us calmly watch out the window!

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'why'.

examples.trans: Why are we going so slowly?
Why are you here?

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

meanings.note: polite to one person, or to several people
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: As you all know...
Does the governor support you?

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('so') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('like that, so') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
That's good like that.
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Он бегает и очень весело играет.
examples.trans: He runs around and plays very merrily.

examples.text: Шеф, почему вы так весело улыбаетесь?
examples.trans: Chef, why are you smiling so cheerfully?

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'лыбаться'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to smile', forming an aspectual pair with 'улыбнуться'. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.

examples.trans: He just sits there smiling.
Why are you smiling?
Nothing! He just sits there smiling.

meanings.en: to have a look, to take a look
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'смотреть'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to have a look', forming an aspectual pair with 'смотреть'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to watch (a film) through') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: May I have a look?
I only had a look.
Can I go and have a look?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Agentive or instrument masculine noun meaning 'yard', declining across all six Russian grammatical cases.

examples.trans: The children are playing in the yard.
At the same time I'll trim the branches in the yard.

examples.text: Вы пенсионерке помогли и двор наш очистили.
examples.trans: You helped a pensioner and cleared our yard.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'neighboring' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.

examples.text: В соседнем зале играет тихая музыка.
examples.trans: Quiet music plays in the neighboring hall.

examples.text: За соседним столиком сидели приятные люди.
examples.trans: Pleasant people were sitting at the next table.
To a guest at the next table.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.text: Слушай, Нина, это же тот самый ресторан!
examples.trans: Listen, Nina, this is that very restaurant!

examples.text: Мы рады видеть вас в нашем ресторане.
examples.trans: We are glad to see you in our restaurant.
They called from the Italian restaurant.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'there'.

examples.trans: They put bad meat in there for you.
Let's go there together.

examples.text: Хочешь, сейчас и тебя туда увезут?
examples.trans: Want them to take you there too right now?

meanings.note: softens a request: только не сердись = just don't be angry

examples.trans: I was only looking.
Just one.
I was only looking!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: What's this?
Look what I've got.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'ехать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to arrive (by vehicle)', paired with 'приезжать'.

examples.trans: Which car did you come in?
Pasha has arrived.

examples.text: Вика, ты на какой машине сегодня приехала?
examples.trans: Vika, which car did you come in today?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'трогий'). Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('strict, stern').

examples.trans: How strict you are, Klavdia Viktorovna.

examples.text: У нас в школе очень строгий директор.
examples.trans: We have a very strict principal at our school.

examples.text: Ой, спина не разгибается! Какая вы строгая, Клавдия Викторовна.
examples.trans: Ow, my back won't straighten! How strict you are, Klavdia Viktorovna.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'верка'). Common feminine noun meaning 'check, inspection, test' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: It was a test.
An inspection is underway at the bank.

examples.text: Эксперты уже начали проверку состояния старой стены.
examples.trans: Experts have already begun checking the condition of the old wall.

meanings.note: emphatic at the start of a sentence
Secondary conversational sense ('? = really?, oh yeah?') (disbelief) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Oh yeah?
Yes, it's me.
Oh yeah? When?

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: That's mine.
And this is for you.
And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.en: special, designed for a particular purpose
meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'special' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.

examples.trans: Calm down, the special operation continues.
A special tool is needed for this.
Everyone down! Special forces at work!

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'service', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('service, duty, work') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Дорожная служба обещала закатать её десять лет назад.
examples.trans: The road service promised to pave it over ten years ago.
He returned from duty late.
Right now we need to call social services.

meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to come', forming an aspectual pair with 'приходить'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: Security will be here any moment.
I'll come tomorrow.

examples.text: Не надо, Самсон. Сейчас придёт охрана.
examples.trans: Don't, Samson. Security will be here any second.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('oneself') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.trans: I'll do it myself.
He knows himself.

examples.text: Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
examples.trans: I'll have a good time on my own.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'звонить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to call', forming an aspectual pair with 'звонить'.

examples.trans: Call me this evening.
I'll call tomorrow.

examples.text: Позвони мне вечером. Договоримся на завтра.
examples.trans: Call me this evening. We'll arrange something for tomorrow.

meanings.note: alone: 'я этого не хочу' = I don't want that

examples.trans: This house.
I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: International noun in '-ция' (from Latin '-tio'), feminine declension. Common feminine noun meaning 'inspection' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Soon the sanitary inspection will arrive.
This is a strict rule of the sanitary inspection.
Soon the restaurant's sanitary inspection will arrive.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'of course'.

examples.trans: Of course I'll help.
Yes, of course.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('they') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.trans: They are building a centre.
History will punish them.

examples.text: Ты преподавай. А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: You teach. And let them build their shopping centres.

meanings.note: + infinitive; agrees with the subject: должна (f)
Secondary conversational sense ('owe') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I have to work.
Greed should be moderate.

examples.text: Жадность, Паша, должна быть умеренная. Комнатной температуры.
examples.trans: Greed, Pasha, should be moderate. Room temperature.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'важать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to respect'.

examples.trans: Respect the court!
I respect you.
I demand silence! Respect the court!

meanings.note: Declinable neuter noun meaning 'rule', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('expression') (by the rules) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: All by the rules.
That's the rule.

examples.text: Всё по правилам, как рыцарский турнир.
examples.trans: All by the rules, like a knights' tournament.

meanings.note: по порядку = in order; всё в порядке = everything is fine

examples.trans: Now let's go through everything in order.
Everything is in complete order.

examples.text: Теперь давай всё по порядку. Скажи мне, сколько ты им должна?
examples.trans: Now let's go through everything in order. Tell me, how much do you owe them?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'now'.

examples.trans: Now I'm the boss.
Now everything's fine.

examples.text: Теперь я начальник нашей стройки. Ты уволен!
examples.trans: Now I'm the boss of our building site. You're fired!

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'cook', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: There is this English chef.

examples.text: Есть такой английский повар. Я по его передачам научусь готовить.
examples.trans: There is this English chef. I will learn to cook from his shows.

examples.text: Я хочу работать поваром в ресторане.
examples.trans: I want to work as a cook in a restaurant.

meanings.note: the present tense is normally left out: я мэр = I am the mayor
Secondary conversational sense ('there is, there are') (present есть; у меня есть = I have) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
future: буду / будешь ... + infinitive

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.
You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'strongly'.

examples.trans: I loved him so much!
The wind is blowing hard outside.

examples.text: Я так два года потеряла. Любила так сильно!
examples.trans: I lost two years like that. I loved him so much!

meanings.en: to run (in various directions or habitually)
meanings.note: вокруг меня бегала = she was running after me

examples.trans: She was running after me.
The children are running around in the yard.

examples.text: Это она со мной познакомилась! Вокруг меня бегала.
examples.trans: She was the one who came up to me! She was running after me.

meanings.note: + 3rd person verb: 'пусть строят' = let them build

examples.trans: Let them build.
Let him come.

examples.text: Ты преподавай. А они пусть строят свои торговые центры.
examples.trans: You teach. And let them build their shopping centres.

meanings.note: the comparative 'быстрее', often as an order
the comparative 'быстрее', often as an order

examples.trans: He drives fast.

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

examples.text: Давай работай быстрее, гости уже давно ждут заказ!
examples.trans: Come on, work faster, the guests have been waiting for their order for a long time!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'around' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: She was running after me (around me).
Look around.
She circled around me like a shark.

meanings.note: large structure such as an office, school, or hall

examples.text: На огромной скорости машина врезалась в здание!
examples.trans: At huge speed the car crashed into the building!
This is an old, beautiful building.

examples.text: Пятнадцать лет мы просим новое здание!
examples.trans: For fifteen years we've been asking for a new building!

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'very'.
Secondary conversational sense ('very much') (with verbs: очень люблю) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.
It's very hard.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

злиться.gloss: to be angry, to get mad

meanings.en: to be angry, to get mad
meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to be angry', forming an aspectual pair with 'разозлиться'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.

examples.text: А знаешь, почему ты так злишься?
examples.trans: And do you know why you are so angry?
Don't be angry with me, please.

examples.text: Хорошо. А знаешь, почему ты так злишься?
examples.trans: Fine. Do you know why you're so angry?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('she') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.trans: She's a lecturer.
I haven't heard of her.

examples.text: Паша, я больше не хочу о ней слышать. Понял?
examples.trans: Pasha, I don't want to hear about her again. Understood?

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates

examples.trans: I don't know.
There wasn't enough money.
Chef, I didn't take it.

meanings.en: to put, to place in an upright position
meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'тавить'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to put', forming an aspectual pair with 'поставить'.

examples.trans: Where should I put the plate?
Put the kettle on the table.

examples.text: Успокойтесь, я ещё сделаю! Куда ставить тарелку?
examples.trans: Calm down, I'll make more! Where should I put the plate?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'car; machine' in everyday Russian.
Secondary conversational sense ('machine') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Is this our car now?
Which car did you come in?
A car. A German one.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'here'.

examples.trans: I'm here.
We live here.
But we're in business here.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Настроение у меня действительно очень хорошее.
examples.trans: My mood really is very good.
This is indeed an important question.
Quiet, stop! It really hurts!

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('cruel, harsh, severe').

examples.text: Анатолий Иванович, вы были слишком жестоки.
examples.trans: Anatoly Ivanovich, you were too harsh.
A cruel person.
I agree, but life can be cruel.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('small, little').

examples.trans: A small house.
One small formality.
There's just one small formality.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'revenge', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: This is revenge.
It was revenge.
Samson, listen. It was revenge.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'fair', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.trans: Dmitry made a fair decision.

examples.text: Это было справедливое наказание для хулиганов.
examples.trans: That was a fair punishment for the troublemakers.

examples.text: Дмитрий, спасибо вам за справедливое решение.
examples.trans: Dmitry, thank you for the fair decision.

meanings.note: in уроки учить / делать уроки, plural
in уроки учить / делать уроки, plural

examples.trans: I'm doing my homework.
The lesson is starting.
Not allowed? All right, I'll go and do my homework.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'for' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: We could open a salon for you.
This is for you.

examples.text: Для вас можно открыть салон красоты.
examples.trans: We could open a beauty salon for you.

meanings.note: showing a lack of respect in a rude or aggressive manner

examples.trans: That was a very insolent act.
What an insolent, vile thief!
Be quiet right now, insolent rump!

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'neighbour', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Hi, neighbours!
This is our neighbour.

examples.text: Соседи, привет! Слушай, дружок, дай свой телефон на минутку.
examples.trans: Hi, neighbours! Listen, buddy, lend me your phone for a minute.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'then'.
Secondary conversational sense ('then, in that case') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Back then I was little.
Then come tomorrow.

examples.text: Я тебе тогда сказал: ты меня ещё поцелуешь.
examples.trans: I told you back then: you'll kiss me one day.

meanings.note: давай + 1st person plural or infinitive
давай + 1st person plural or infinitive

examples.trans: Let's talk.
He gives me a book.

examples.text: Давай мы его уволим, а тебя на его место назначим.
examples.trans: Let's fire him and put you in his place.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'покойно'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: You'll do everything calmly.
He sat calmly.

examples.text: Его не будет часа два. Вы спокойно всё сделаете.
examples.trans: He'll be gone for about two hours. You'll do everything calmly.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'мотреть'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to look', forming an aspectual pair with 'посмотреть'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to watch') (TV, a film) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Look what I've got.
I'm watching TV.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'window' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: He is looking out the window.
Open the window, please.

examples.text: Все видели, как ты из окна летел.
examples.trans: Everyone saw you fly out the window.
